claim: The number of retracted scientific articles has been increasing.
source: The number of retracted scientific articles has been increasing.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the abstract without specific data provided in this sentence, but is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most retractions are associated with research misconduct.
source: Most retractions are associated with research misconduct
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in the introduction.

claim: Papers retracted due to misconduct accounted for approximately $58 million in direct funding by the NIH between 1992 and 2012.
source: We found that papers retracted due to misconduct accounted for approximately $58 million in direct funding by the NIH between 1992 and 2012
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of retracted manuscripts and NIH funding data from ExPORTER database.

claim: Papers retracted due to misconduct represented less than 1% of the NIH budget between 1992 and 2012.
source: papers retracted due to misconduct accounted for approximately $58 million in direct funding by the NIH between 1992 and 2012, less than 1% of the NIH budget over this period
evidence: This is calculated from the $58 million finding relative to total NIH budget.

claim: Each retracted article accounted for a mean of $392,582 in direct costs (SD $423,256).
source: Each of these articles accounted for a mean of $392,582 in direct costs (SD $423,256).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the analyzed data on attributable costs.

claim: Researchers experienced a median 91.8% decrease in publication output after censure by the ORI.
source: Researchers experienced a median 91.8% decrease in publication output and large declines in funding after censure by the ORI.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publication records before and after ORI findings.

claim: Researchers experienced large declines in funding after censure by the ORI.
source: Researchers experienced a median 91.8% decrease in publication output and large declines in funding after censure by the ORI.
evidence: This is based on analysis of NIH funding data before and after ORI findings.

claim: Honest retractions resulting from scientific error represent a mechanism for correction of the literature.
source: Honest retractions resulting from scientific error represent a mechanism for correction of the literature (Casadevall et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The majority of retractions result from scientific misconduct.
source: A recent study of the causes for retraction of scientific articles found that the majority of these result from scientific misconduct (Fang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Hundreds of thousands of patients have been placed at risk of improper medical care due to enrollment in fraudulent studies or the administration of treatment based on fraudulent studies.
source: Some studies indicate that hundreds of thousands of patients have been placed at risk of improper medical care due to enrollment in fraudulent studies or the administration of treatment based on fraudulent studies (Steen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Pressure to 'publish or perish' during times of scarce resources, increased competition and the winner-take-all economics of research may contribute to an atmosphere in which some individuals are tempted to commit misconduct.
source: It has been suggested that pressure to 'publish or perish' during times of scarce resources, increased competition and the winner-take-all economics of research may contribute to an atmosphere in which some individuals are tempted to commit misconduct (Casadevall and Fang, 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Whether the actual frequency of misconduct is increasing is unknown.
source: Whether the actual frequency of misconduct is increasing is unknown (Fanelli, 2013; Steen et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty and cites relevant literature.

claim: Discovery of research misconduct has serious consequences for those who perpetrate it.
source: It is generally accepted that discovery of research misconduct has serious consequences for those who perpetrate it.
evidence: This is presented as generally accepted knowledge in the field.

claim: The consequences of misconduct and other costs of misconduct to society have not been systematically studied or quantified.
source: However, such consequences, as well as other costs of misconduct to society, have not been systematically studied or quantified.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: 291 articles originating from the United States and published between 1992 and 2012 were retracted for research misconduct.
source: We examined the text of 291 articles originating from the United States and published between 1992 and 2012 that were retracted for research misconduct (Fang et al., 2012)
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study, derived from a prior publication.

claim: 95.9% of the analyzed retracted articles were retracted due to data falsification or fabrication.
source: Of the articles included in this analysis, 95.9% were retracted due to data falsification or fabrication

claim: NIH funding was identified for 149 of 291 retracted articles.
source: Through this method we were able to identify NIH funding for 149 of 291 retracted articles

claim: The median attributable cost per retracted article was $239,381.
source: with a median attributable cost of $239,381 per retracted article

claim: The mean attributable cost per retracted article was $392,582.

source: Most of the funding for this article came from a large R01 grant that appears to have supported only this single paper.

claim: Questions regarding the research by the Potti group first arose in 2007.
source: Questions regarding the research by this group first arose in 2007

source: it is likely that the subsequent investigations had a negative effect on the productivity of the grant

source: Impact factor exhibits a positive correlation with articles retracted for research misconduct or error (Fang and Casadevall, 2011; Fang et al., 2012).

claim: Impact factor correlates with attributable cost.
source: Here we determined that impact factor also correlates with attributable cost (Figure 1C)

claim: Multiplying $425,073 by the total number of articles retracted due to scientific misconduct in the United States (291) yields a value of $123.7 million, which might be considered an estimate of the total NIH funds directly spent on known biomedical research retracted due to misconduct over the past 20 years.
source: Multiplying this number by the total number of articles retracted due to scientific misconduct in the United States (291) yields a value of $123.7 million, which might be considered an estimate of the total NIH funds directly spent on known biomedical research retracted due to misconduct over the past 20 years.
evidence: This is an extrapolation calculation to estimate total costs.

claim: Even when deliberately overestimating the funding contributions by totaling all grants that provided any support for papers retracted due to misconduct, the figure ($1.67 billion in actual funds, $2.32 billion in 2012 dollars) is still less than 1% of the NIH budget over this time period.
source: Additionally, even when deliberately overestimating the funding contributions to this research by totaling all grants that provided any support for papers retracted due to misconduct, the figure ($1.67 billion in actual funds, $2.32 billion in 2012 dollars) is still less than 1% of the NIH budget over this time period.

source: A meta-analysis of survey data indicates that approximately 2% of scientists admit to data falsification or manipulation on at least one occasion (Fanelli, 2009)

source: whereas less than 0.02% of published data are retracted due to fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism (Claxton, 2005; Fang et al., 2012)

source: Even with this correction, research misconduct would only account for approximately 1.5% of the NIH research budget since 1992.

source: Thus, considering every dollar spent on retracted publications to be completely wasted may result in an overestimation of the true cost of misconduct.

source: The financial costs of research misconduct extend beyond the grants supporting the work.

source: Investigations of misconduct allegations are costly for institutions.

source: In analyzing a single case at the Roswell Park Cancer Institute, Michalek et al. (2010) identified many financial costs of research misconduct, including legal and consulting fees, salaries for faculty and witnesses involved in the investigation, institutional review board costs and other expenses, with estimates exceeding $500,000, greater than the median attributable cost to research funding sources.

source: Gammon and Franzini (2013) analyzed 17 cases using a mixed methods model to conclude that ORI cases incur financial costs ranging from approximately $100,000 to $2 million.

This indirect financial cost due to the reverberations of fraud throughout the research community might be even greater than the cost of the retracted research itself.
